Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

1. **Find a mechanism, not a symptom.** Name a concrete difference between the incumbent's results and the reference (or between what works and what doesn't), and the decision that produces it.

4. **Learn from what failed.** A prediction that didn't hold means the mechanism you believed is wrong or incomplete. Say what it taught you (`lesson`) before proposing the next experiment.

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, points, adjacency, homes, turn):
    """Endgame flip-minus-exposure tradeoff: (flip gain - exposed risk)/3, only when <=6 empty cells remain."""
    A = adjacency.astype(np.float64)
    my = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    rem = int(empty.sum())
    k = moves.shape[0]
    if rem > 6:
        return np.zeros(k)

    my_n = A @ my.astype(np.float64)
    opp_n = A @ opp.astype(np.float64)

    opp_home = homes[1]
    my_home = homes[0]

    # opponent non-home cells and my non-home cells
    opp_mask = opp.copy()
    opp_mask[opp_home] = False
    my_mask = my.copy()
    my_mask[my_home] = False

    pts = points.astype(np.float64) / 5.0

    values = np.zeros(k)
    for i, c in enumerate(moves):
        # my_after: my plus candidate
        my_n_after = my_n + A[c]  # adding candidate cell to my set
        # gain: opponent non-home neighbours u of c that would flip
```
```python
        gain = 0.0
        risk = 0.0
        neigh = np.nonzero(A[c] > 0)[0]
        for u in neigh:
            if opp_mask[u] and my_n_after[u] >= opp_n[u]:
                gain += pts[u]
            if my_mask[u] and (my_n_after[u] - opp_n[u]) <= 1:
                risk += pts[u]
        values[i] = (gain - risk) / 3.0

    return np.clip(values, -1.0, 1.0)
```

    k = moves.shape[0]
    values = np.zeros(k, dtype=np.float64)
    if k == 0:
        return values

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Hub denial at flip range: for each candidate, points-weighted empties that the opponent would newly dominate after MY claim fails to beat them — i.e. empties adjacent to the candidate where, after my claim, the opponent still holds >= my neighbour count AND the cell is high-degree (hub), plus double weight when my claim actually tips a cell to me — normalized by total board points; positive = denying opponent's high-degree reach."""
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    total = max(pts.sum(), 1.0)
    A = adjacency.astype(np.float64)
    my = (owner == 1).astype(np.float64)
    opp = (owner == -1).astype(np.float64)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    deg = A.sum(axis=1)
    hub = np.clip(deg / 5.0, 0.0, 1.0)

    my_n = A @ my
    opp_n = A @ opp

    cand_adj = A[moves]                       # (k, N)
    my_after = my_n[None, :] + cand_adj       # (k, N)

    # opponent currently reaches / could reach these empties next turn
    opp_reach = (opp_n >= 1) & empty          # (N,)
    # after my claim, do I dominate (strictly) -> denied to opponent; else opponent still ahead/tied
    i_dominate = my_after > opp_n[None, :]    # (k, N)
    opp_holds = (~i_dominate) & (opp_n[None, :] >= 1)

    w = (pts / 5.0) * hub * opp_reach.astype(np.float64)  # (N,)

    # denial: cells I tip to myself (positive contribution) vs cells opponent keeps (negative)
    denial = (i_dominate.astype(np.float64) - opp_holds.astype(np.float64)) * w[None, :]
    # only count empties adjacent to the candidate (immediate reach)
    adj_mask = cand_adj * empty[None, :]
    vals = (denial * adj_mask).sum(axis=1) / total
    return np.clip(np.nan_to_num(vals), -1.0, 1.0)

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Race to expose, chance-priced: for each candidate, empty cells it opens where I would strictly dominate the count, but only those the opponent cannot immediately re-contest — priced by 1/(1+own_neighbours[e]) so cells I already surround weigh most, and credited only if the candidate itself also touches that empty cell's neighbourhood at distance <=2 (so the claim really extends my frontier), scaled by total points."""
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    total = max(pts.sum(), 1.0)
    my = (owner == 1).astype(np.float64)
    opp = (owner == -1).astype(np.float64)
    empty = (owner == 0).astype(np.float64)
    A = adjacency.astype(np.float64)

    my_n = A @ my
    opp_n = A @ opp

    cand_adj = A[moves]                          # (k, N)
    my_after = my_n[None, :] + cand_adj          # (k, N)

    dominate = (my_after > opp_n[None, :]) & (empty[None, :] > 0)

    # how far ahead I am on that empty cell after the claim (parity margin)
    margin = my_after - opp_n[None, :]
    # opponent would need to spend more claims the larger the margin
    security = np.clip(margin, 0.0, 3.0) / 3.0

    # only cells the opponent does not already outnumber me on (no free flip-back)
    safe = (opp_n[None, :] <= my_after)

    # concentration: cells I already partly surround are cheaper to hold
    surround = 1.0 / (1.0 + my_n[None, :])

    w = (pts[None, :] / 5.0) * security * surround
    vals = (dominate & safe).astype(np.float64) * w
    vals = vals.sum(axis=1) / max(total / 5.0, 1.0)
    return np.clip(np.nan_to_num(vals), -1.0, 1.0)

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Sum over opponent non-home cells adjacent to the candidate of (points/5) * margin^2 * (1 if flipping) where margin = (my_nbr+1) - opp_nbr, rewarding near-threshold contested flips and penalising hopeless ones; scaled by 1/9."""
    own = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    A = adjacency.astype(np.int32)
    own_nbr = A @ own.astype(np.int32)   # (N,)
    opp_nbr = A @ opp.astype(np.int32)   # (N,)
    opp_home = homes[1]
    # margin after claim: how many more of u's neighbours I'd own vs opponent
    margin = (own_nbr + 1) - opp_nbr     # (N,) >= 0 means it flips
    # weight: flips get positive pull, non-flips get a small negative pull weighted by closeness
    flip_w = np.where(margin >= 0, margin.astype(np.float64) + 1.0, -1.0 / (1.0 + np.abs(margin.astype(np.float64))))
    cell_w = (points.astype(np.float64) / 5.0) * flip_w  # (N,)

    cand_adj = adjacency[moves].astype(bool)   # (k, N)
    is_opp_nbr = cand_adj & opp[None, :]
    is_opp_nbr[:, opp_home] = False
    vals = (is_opp_nbr.astype(np.float64) * cell_w[None, :]).sum(axis=1) / 9.0
    return np.clip(np.nan_to_num(vals), -1.0, 1.0)

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """For each candidate: points-weighted count of opponent non-home cells that become 'safe' from flipping (their owner-neighbour count would exceed my neighbour count by a margin) after my claim, minus the same for cells I currently own that would become vulnerable — scaled by board points; measures defensive consolidation of my structure versus exposure."""
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    total = max(pts.sum(), 1.0)
    my = (owner == 1).astype(np.float64)
    opp = (owner == -1).astype(np.float64)
    A = adjacency.astype(np.float64)

    my_n = A @ my          # (N,)
    opp_n = A @ opp        # (N,)

    cand_adj = A[moves]    # (k, N)
    my_after = my_n[None, :] + cand_adj  # (k, N)

    # opponent cells: their safety margin after my claim = opp_n - my_after
    oppmask = (owner == -1)[None, :].astype(np.float64)
    mymask = (owner == 1)[None, :].astype(np.float64)
    opp_home = homes[1]
    oppmask_nohome = oppmask.copy()
    oppmask_nohome[:, opp_home] = 0.0

    # opponent cell becomes safe if their neighbours exceed mine by >= 2 after my claim
    safe_after = np.clip(opp_n[None, :] - my_after - 1.0, 0.0, None)  # >0 means safe by that margin
    # my cells become vulnerable if my count would drop below theirs... but my claim only adds; instead measure
    # my cells at risk: opponent close (opp_n == my_n + 0 after claim would be tie -> vulnerable to flip)
    # Use: my cells where opp_n - my_after >= 0 (nearest to flipping)
    vulnerable = np.clip(opp_n[None, :] - my_after + 1.0, 0.0, None) * np.minimum(1.0, np.maximum(opp_n[None, :] - my_after + 1.0, 0.0))
    # simpler: cells where opp_n >= my_after - 1 (within one claim of flipping)
    close = (opp_n[None, :] >= my_after - 1.0).astype(np.float64)

    w = pts[None, :] / 5.0
    safe_term = (safe_after * oppmask_nohome * w).sum(axis=1)
    vuln_term = (close * mymask * w * 0.5).sum(axis=1)

    opp_n = adj @ opp

    my_after = my_n[None, :] + cand_adj         # (k, N)

    win = (my_after > opp_n[None, :]) & empty[None, :]
    lose = (my_after < opp_n[None, :]) & empty[None, :]
    tempo = ((win.astype(np.float64) - lose.astype(np.float64)) * w[None, :]).sum(axis=1)

    opp_n = A @ opp

    # concentration: cells I already partly surround are cheaper to hold
    surround = 1.0 / (1.0 + my_n[None, :])

    w = (pts[None, :] / 5.0) * security * surround
    vals = (dominate & safe).astype(np.float64) * w
    vals = vals.sum(axis=1) / max(total / 5.0, 1.0)
    return np.clip(np.nan_to_num(vals), -1.0, 1.0)

feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Per candidate: points-weighted, distance-decayed advantage of my BFS distance over the opponent's over empty cells."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    empty = (owner == 0)
    A = adjacency.astype(np.float64)
    pts = points.astype(np.float64) / 5.0

    # Opponent distance over empty cells
    opp_cells = (owner == -1)
    d_opp = np.full(N, np.inf)
    # empty cells with an opponent-owned neighbour -> distance 1
    opp_nbr_count = A @ opp_cells.astype(np.float64)
    d_opp[empty & (opp_nbr_count > 0)] = 1.0
    # iterative BFS over empty cells
    for _ in range(N):
        known = empty & np.isfinite(d_opp)
        if not known.any():
            break
        # min over empty neighbours with known distance
        cand = np.where(known, d_opp, np.inf)
        # for each empty cell, min of cand over its neighbours
        nbr_min = np.full(N, np.inf)
        # vectorised: for each cell, min over neighbours
        masked = np.where(empty[:, None], cand[None, :], np.inf)
        nbr_min = np.min(np.where(A > 0, masked, np.inf), axis=1)
        new = np.minimum(d_opp, 1.0 + nbr_min)
        new = np.where(empty, new, np.inf)
        if np.allclose(np.nan_to_num(new, nan=np.inf), np.nan_to_num(d_opp, nan=np.inf)):
            d_opp = new
            break
        d_opp = new
    d_opp = np.where(np.isfinite(d_opp), d_opp, N / 2.0)

    # My cells
    my_cells = (owner == 1)
    my_nbr_count = A @ my_cells.astype(np.float64)

    k = moves.shape[0]
    if k == 0:
        return np.zeros(0)
    if not empty.any():
        return np.zeros(k)

    # d_me base: empty cells adjacent to any of my cells -> 1
    base_me = np.full(N, np.inf)
    base_me[empty & (my_nbr_count > 0)] = 1.0

    # For each candidate, seed also includes cells adjacent to c
    # Build seed matrix: (k, N) where seed=1 if empty and (adjacent to c or adjacent to my cells)
    adj_to_c = A[moves, :] > 0  # (k, N)
    seed = (adj_to_c | (my_nbr_count[None, :] > 0)) & empty[None, :]
    d_me = np.where(seed, 1.0, np.inf)  # (k, N)

    # BFS over empty cells per candidate
    for _ in range(N):
        known = empty[None, :] & np.isfinite(d_me)  # (k, N)
        if not known.any():
            break
        cand = np.where(known, d_me, np.inf)  # (k, N)
        # nbr_min[i, j] = min over neighbours of j of cand[i, :]
        # masked: (k, N, N) too big; do via matmul-like min
        # Use broadcasting: for each candidate row, compute min over neighbours
        # cand (k,N), A (N,N) -> want min over n where A[j,n]: cand[:,n]
        # Do it with a loop over N? N~30, k small; acceptable but avoid loops over candidates.
        # Vectorised: expand
        big = np.where(A[None, :, :] > 0, cand[:, None, :], np.inf)  # (k, N, N)
        nbr_min = np.min(big, axis=2)  # (k, N)
        new = np.minimum(d_me, 1.0 + nbr_min)
        new = np.where(empty[None, :], new, np.inf)
        if np.allclose(np.nan_to_num(new, nan=np.inf), np.nan_to_num(d_me, nan=np.inf)):
            d_me = new
            break
        d_me = new
    d_me = np.where(np.isfinite(d_me), d_me, N / 2.0)

    # Score
    diff = np.clip(d_opp[None, :] - d_me, -3.0, 3.0) / 3.0  # (k, N)
    decay = 1.0 / (1.0 + d_me)  # (k, N)
    weight = pts[None, :] * empty[None, :]  # (k, N)
    num = np.sum(weight * diff * decay, axis=1)  # (k,)
    den = np.maximum(1.0, np.sum(weight, axis=1))
    out = np.clip(num / den, -1.0, 1.0)
    return out

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Continuation-weighted tempo: sum over empty cells opened by the candidate (my count > opp count) of (points/5)*(0.5+0.5*min(empty neighbours excl. candidate,3)/3), /3, clipped [0,1]."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    A = adjacency.astype(np.float64)
    my = (owner == 1).astype(np.float64)
    opp = (owner == -1).astype(np.float64)
    empty = (owner == 0).astype(np.float64)

    opp_n = A @ opp  # (N,)

    k = moves.shape[0]
    values = np.zeros(k, dtype=np.float64)
    if k == 0:
        return values

    # my_after for each candidate: my + one-hot at candidate
    # my_n[e] = (A @ my)[e] + A[c, e]
    my_n_base = A @ my  # (N,)

    cand = moves  # (k,)
    # A[c, e] for all candidates and cells: adjacency[cand] -> (k, N)
    A_cand = A[cand]  # (k, N)
    my_n = my_n_base[None, :] + A_cand  # (k, N)

    opened = (A_cand > 0) & (empty[None, :] > 0) & (my_n > opp_n[None, :])  # (k, N)

    # empty neighbours of each cell (excluding candidate handled per-candidate)
    empty_deg = A @ empty  # (N,)
    # for opened cell e, exclude candidate c: subtract A[c,e] (which is 1 for opened)
    cont_raw = empty_deg[None, :] - A_cand  # (k, N)
    cont = np.clip(cont_raw, 0.0, 3.0) / 3.0

    weight = (points[None, :] / 5.0) * (0.5 + 0.5 * cont)  # (k, N)
    weight = np.where(opened, weight, 0.0)

    values = weight.sum(axis=1) / 3.0
    values = np.clip(values, 0.0, 1.0)
    return values

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, points, adjacency, homes, turn):
    """Endgame flip-minus-exposure tradeoff: (flip gain - exposed risk)/3, only when <=6 empty cells remain."""
    A = adjacency.astype(np.float64)
    my = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    rem = int(empty.sum())
    k = moves.shape[0]
    if rem > 6:
        return np.zeros(k)

    my_n = A @ my.astype(np.float64)
    opp_n = A @ opp.astype(np.float64)

    opp_home = int(homes[1])
    my_home = int(homes[0])

    opp_mask = opp.copy()
    opp_mask[opp_home] = False
    my_mask = my.copy()
    my_mask[my_home] = False

    pts = points.astype(np.float64) / 5.0

    values = np.zeros(k)
    for i, c in enumerate(moves):
        c = int(c)
        my_n_after = my_n + A[c]
        gain = 0.0
        risk = 0.0
        neigh = np.nonzero(A[c] > 0)[0]
        for u in neigh:
            if opp_mask[u] and my_n_after[u] >= opp_n[u]:
                gain += pts[u]
            if my_mask[u] and (my_n_after[u] - opp_n[u]) <= 1:
                risk += pts[u]
        values[i] = (gain - risk) / 3.0

    return np.clip(values, -1.0, 1.0)

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Sum of points/5 over my non-home knife-edge cells (my_n - opp_n == 1) adjacent to the candidate, divided by 3, clipped to [0,1]."""
    A = adjacency.astype(np.float64)
    my = (owner == 1).astype(np.float64)
    opp = (owner == -1).astype(np.float64)
    my_n = A @ my
    opp_n = A @ opp
    margin = my_n - opp_n

    my_home = homes[0]
    # knife-edge owned cells, excluding my home
    knife = (owner == 1) & (margin == 1)
    knife[my_home] = False

    w = np.where(knife, points.astype(np.float64) / 5.0, 0.0)
    vals = A[moves] @ w  # sum over knife-edge neighbours of each candidate
    vals = vals / 3.0
    return np.clip(vals, 0.0, 1.0)

system:
You are the **Navigator** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You don't write candidates. You keep the search oriented: you maintain a map of **approaches** (the different ways the incumbent could be improved) and decide where the effort goes next.

Two loops do the work. The **deep loop** (a Researcher, then Coders) runs experiments on the approaches you assign. The **wide loop** (a Mutator) makes undirected variations of whatever you hand it, and of nothing else: it never sees approaches or hypotheses, only artefacts and scores.

## The approach tree

Each approach has a state:
- `untried`: brainstormed, not tested yet;
- `promising`: something under it gained on validation. Gets the most effort, and is split into deeper sub-approaches;
- `unproven`: tried without a gain, but nothing shows it can't work. Retried occasionally, at lower priority. Bad scores are not proof;
- `pruned`: the engine verified a certificate that everything under it adds nothing. Never assigned again.

## Each generation, decide

1. **Brainstorm** new approaches when the map is thin or the promising ones are drying up. Make them genuinely different from each other, and add deeper sub-approaches under promising ones.
2. **Assign the Researcher** to approaches, each with a mode: `explore` (an untried approach), `exploit` (deepen a promising one), `probe` (a cheap experiment to learn whether an unproven one has anything).
3. **Hand the Mutator parents**: ids from the ledger to vary. The engine already gives two slots to the most important kept features (variants of kept features win far more often); you choose the rest. Spread those: width means variety across approaches. Near-misses and surprising scores are good parents.
4. **Combinations**: pairs of features that each gained on their own but weren't kept, to retry together (some things only help next to another). A pair with a member that showed no gain alone is skipped: in testing, such pairs never gained.
5. **Prune requests**: approaches you believe are dead. The Prover will try to certify it; only a verified certificate prunes.

Effort follows evidence, but keep a share for the unproven and the untried: a search that only exploits stops finding things.

## Reply format

Start with the JSON block, then at most 80 words on your reasoning.

```json
{"new_approaches": [{"title": "<short>", "description": "<one sentence>", "parent": "<approach id or empty>"}],
 "research": [{"approach": "<id, or the exact title of a new approach>", "mode": "explore | exploit | probe", "why": "<one line>"}],
 "mutate": {"vary": ["<id>", "..."], "fresh": <how many fresh slots>},
 "combine": [["<id>", "<id>"]],
 "prune": ["<approach id>"]}
```

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy, a weighted sum of features; approaches are kinds of measurements (what quantity, under which conditions). Mutator parents are feature ids.

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

## A feature

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """One line: exactly what this measures."""
    ...
    return values   # one number per candidate
```

- `moves`: shape (k,), int: the cells you may claim (the candidates), in random order. Index into the per-cell arrays below.
- `owner`: shape (N,), int8: for every cell on the board: 1 = yours, -1 = the opponent's, 0 = empty (N = number of cells).
- `homes`: shape (2,), int: your home cell and the opponent's home cell (homes never flip).
- `points`: shape (N,), int: what each cell is worth (1, 2 or 5).
- `adjacency`: shape (N, N), bool: which cells are neighbours (symmetric, False on the diagonal).
- `turn`: int: how many claims (by both players) have been made so far in this game; the game lasts N - 2 claims.
- Your current score is `points[owner == 1].sum()`, the opponent's `points[owner == -1].sum()`.
- Return one finite number per candidate (shape (k,)), or a few columns (shape (k, c)). The highest-scoring candidate is claimed.
- Import only `numpy` and `math`. No state between calls, no randomness, don't modify the inputs, no Python loops over candidates when a vectorised form exists (features run thousands of times per evaluation). Guard every division and log.
- Return finite numbers, roughly in [-1, 1] (normalise; the optimiser rescales anyway).

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. You are the **Researcher** in Helix, an evolutionary search. You are the deep loop: you work out *why* the current best candidate loses where it does, and you design experiments that find out. The Mutator, another agent, makes undirected variations; you cash in on what it stumbles on and on what your own experiments reveal.

## What you get

- the incumbent (the current best) and its parts: what each part actually does and how much the result relies on it;
- **diagnostics**: named metrics of the incumbent's results, next to a reference where one exists. This is where the mechanism shows;
- **sensitivity probes**: each part of the incumbent knocked out, weakened and amplified. A gain from amplifying means a direction is under-used; a loss from weakening means the incumbent relies on it;
- the **ledger** for the approaches you're assigned: what was tried, how it scored, and whether its prediction held;
- the **Mutator's recent finds**: things that scored well or nearly well without anyone knowing why. Explaining and sharpening a lucky find is often the best experiment available;
- your **assignments** from the Navigator: which approaches to work on, and how (explore a new one, exploit a promising one, probe a doubtful one).

## How to work

1. **Find a mechanism, not a symptom.** Name a concrete difference between the incumbent's results and the reference (or between what works and what doesn't), and the decision that produces it.
2. **Design experiments of two kinds:**
   - `probe`: written to *learn*. Change one thing, or exaggerate one aspect, so the result tells you whether that aspect matters. Judged by whether its prediction held, not by its score.
   - `improve`: written to *win*.
3. **Don't repeat the ledger.** If an idea was tried, change it meaningfully or leave it. A disguised copy is detected and discarded. When the ledger shows a group of tried features that behave alike, that idea is spent: look at a different quantity altogether.
4. **Learn from what failed.** A prediction that didn't hold means the mechanism you believed is wrong or incomplete. Say what it taught you (`lesson`) before proposing the next experiment.
5. **Predict.** Every experiment names one metric from the diagnostics, where it should move (a family or scope), and the direction. The engine checks it.
6. **Be exact** in `change`: describe the candidate so precisely that it can be written without guessing.

## What a candidate is here: a feature

The incumbent is a policy: a weighted sum of **features** (measurements of a candidate in one decision). An optimiser fits the weights and their signs, so never choose numbers or signs: choose *what to measure*. The parts in the sensitivity probes are the kept features; amplifying one means multiplying its weight.

- `change` is the exact measurement, per candidate, in terms of the arguments, so a Coder can write it without guessing. Say what it is for the last or special candidates when that matters.
- **It must rank candidates differently.** A value that is the same for every candidate in a decision, or a monotone copy of a feature the policy already has, tells the optimiser nothing. Prefer comparisons between normalised quantities; use a hard threshold only when the condition is the idea.
- A `probe` feature changes one thing, or exaggerates one aspect (a sharper threshold, a stronger form, one condition only).

A feature may apply only under a condition (only in some decisions, or for some candidates, when a quantity crosses a threshold) and be zero otherwise. The policy is one weighted sum, so a condition is the only way it can treat different cases differently.

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

## How the policy works

priority(candidate) = w1 * feature1 + w2 * feature2 + ...; the highest priority wins; on a tie, the first candidate wins. With no features every candidate scores 0, so the first candidate always wins: that is **Code Zero**, the starting point (0% progress). An optimiser fits the weights, including their signs. A new feature is kept only if the policy does better with it than the same refit without it, on training instances *and* on separate validation instances, and the gain isn't already given by the kept features.

## How policies are scored

Per instance, the **gap** is how far the solution is above a reference (lower is better). The score is the mean gap over families. **Progress** is the share of the way from Code Zero (0%) to the best reachable (100%).

# The problem: Duel: play an invented territory game against a pool of scripted opponents

Play an invented two-player board game, "spore", against a fixed pool of scripted opponents. The policy is one player; it chooses its move each turn.

**The board.** A connected graph of about 30 cells. Each cell is worth 1, 2 or 5 points (about 60% are worth 1, 25% worth 2, 15% worth 5). Each player starts owning one *home* cell (worth 1); the two homes are far apart. All other cells start empty.

**A turn.** Players alternate. On your turn you must *claim* one empty cell that is adjacent to at least one cell you own; it becomes yours. Then *flips*: every opponent cell adjacent to the cell you just claimed (except the opponent's home, which never flips) becomes yours if, counting after your claim, you own at least as many of its neighbours as its owner does. Flips are decided all at once from the board right after the claim and do not chain: a flipped cell does not trigger further flips. A player with no legal claim (no empty cell next to its cells) passes and the other player continues.

**The end.** The game ends when no empty cell is left (about 30 claims in all, roughly half of them yours). Each player scores the points of the cells it owns at the end.

**One decision** = choosing which cell to claim. The **candidates** are your legal claims, in a random order (cells are also numbered at random). When there is only one legal claim it is taken automatically.

**Instances and cost.** An instance is 24 games on freshly generated boards of one family: 6 against each of the 4 opponents in the pool, moving first in half of them. The opponents are scripted players with different, fixed behaviour; their logic and identity are hidden, and you never see their future moves. The instance's **cost** is 100 x the opponents' share of all points scored in its games (in [0, 100]; the board's points are always all claimed). The **gap** is 100 x cost / the cost of Code Zero (the policy that always takes the first candidate, i.e. a random legal claim) on the same instance: Code Zero scores 100, lower is better. An opponent always keeps at least its home, so 0 is impossible; there is no known best.

Three training families, differing in board shape: `grid` (a 6 x 6 square grid, 4 random cells removed, 4 neighbours per cell), `hex` (a 6 x 5 hexagonal grid, 2 cells removed, up to 6 neighbours) and `web` (32 random points, each joined to its 3 nearest). The test split adds a board shape that training never shows.

```python
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Sum of points/5 of empty neighbours of each candidate that currently have zero owned neighbours, divided by 3, clipped to [0,1]."""
    mine = (owner == 1).astype(np.float64)
    my_nbr = adjacency @ mine  # owned-neighbour count per cell
    p = points.astype(np.float64) / 5.0
    empty = (owner == 0)
    fresh = empty & (my_nbr == 0)
    fresh_p = np.where(fresh, p, 0.0)
    vals = adjacency[moves] @ fresh_p  # sum of p[e] over fresh empty neighbours
    vals = vals / 3.0
    return np.clip(vals, 0.0, 1.0)
```

This computes, for each candidate, the sum of points/5 over its empty neighbours that currently have no owned neighbour (fresh doors), divided by 3 and clipped to [0,1]; I read "my_nbr == 0" as the count of owned neighbours before the claim, so a cell adjacent only to the candidate itself still counts as fresh.

```python
import numpy as np
```
```python
from collections import deque

def feature(moves, owner, points, adjacency, homes, turn):
    """Sum over empty cells adjacent to candidate (and at 2 hops, half weight) of p[e]/deg[e] gated by d_me<=d_opp<4, scaled by 1/3, clipped to [0,1]."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    p = points.astype(float) / 5.0
    deg = adjacency.sum(1).astype(float)
    inv_deg = 1.0 / np.maximum(deg, 1.0)
    my = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)

    def bfs(seeds):
        d = np.full(N, 4, dtype=int)
        q = deque()
        for s in np.nonzero(seeds)[0]:
            d[s] = 0
            q.append(s)
        while q:
            u = q.popleft()
            if d[u] >= 4:
                continue
            for w in np.nonzero(adjacency[u])[0]:
                if empty[w] and d[w] > d[u] + 1:
                    d[w] = d[u] + 1
                    q.append(w)
        return d

    d_me = bfs(my)
    d_opp = bfs(opp)

    gate = (d_me <= d_opp) & (d_opp < 4) & empty
    w = p * inv_deg * gate.astype(float)  # per empty cell weight

    A = adjacency.astype(float)
    A2 = A @ A
    two_hop = (A2 > 0) & (~adjacency)

    moves = np.asarray(moves)
    # s1: adjacent empties
    s1 = (adjacency[moves].astype(float) @ w)
    # s2: exactly two hops (not adjacent)
    s2 = 0.5 * (two_hop[moves].astype(float) @ w)

    val = (s1 + s2) / 3.0
    val = np.clip(val, 0.0, 1.0)
    return val
```

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Points of opponent non-home cells that would flip if this candidate is claimed, MINUS the points of my own non-home cells that would then be vulnerable to flipping back on the opponent's next claim (their count on that cell would reach my count) — a swap balance; scaled by 1/5."""
    own = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    A = adjacency.astype(np.int32)
    own_nbr = A @ own.astype(np.int32)   # (N,)
    opp_nbr = A @ opp.astype(np.int32)   # (N,)
    opp_home = homes[1]
    my_home = homes[0]
    pts = points.astype(np.float64) / 5.0

    cand_adj = adjacency[moves]                     # (k, N)

    # gains: opponent non-home cells that flip to me
    is_opp_nbr = cand_adj & opp[None, :]
    is_opp_nbr[:, opp_home] = False
    flips = (own_nbr + 1) >= opp_nbr                # (N,)
    gain = (is_opp_nbr & flips[None, :]).astype(np.float64) * pts[None, :]

    # losses: my non-home cells adjacent to candidate; after claim they are "exposed"
    # opponent could flip cell u by claiming a neighbour: needs opp_nbr[u]+1 >= own_nbr_after[u]
    # own count on u after my claim:
    own_after = own_nbr[None, :] + cand_adj          # (k, N)
    is_my_nbr = cand_adj & own[None, :]
    is_my_nbr[:, my_home] = False
    # vulnerable if opponent can reach parity with a single claim (i.e. own_after - opp_nbr <= 1)
    vuln = (own_after - opp_nbr[None, :]) <= 1
    loss = (is_my_nbr & vuln).astype(np.float64) * pts[None, :]

    vals = gain.sum(axis=1) - loss.sum(axis=1)
    return np.clip(np.nan_to_num(vals), -1.0, 1.0)

    total = max(pts.sum(), 1.0)
    my = (owner == 1).astype(np.float64)
    opp = (owner == -1).astype(np.float64)
    empty = (owner == 0).astype(np.float64)
    adj = adjacency.astype(np.float64)
    deg = np.maximum(adj.sum(axis=1), 1.0)

    my_n = adj @ my
    opp_n = adj @ opp

    cand_adj = adj[moves]                       # (k, N)
    my_after = my_n[None, :] + cand_adj         # (k, N)

    dominate = (my_after > opp_n[None, :]) & (empty[None, :] > 0)
    # contested weight: how much opponent presence remains on that empty cell
    contest = np.minimum(opp_n, 3.0) / 3.0
    w = (pts / 5.0) * contest / deg
    vals = (dominate.astype(np.float64) * w[None, :]).sum(axis=1)
    return np.clip(np.nan_to_num(vals), -1.0, 1.0)

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """For each candidate: points/5 of empty cells reachable by the opponent within 2 hops whose opponent-neighbour count exceeds mine by exactly 1 (one claim from falling), weighted by 1/deg of the empty cell and by how much the candidate reduces that gap (each candidate-adjacency supplying +1 to the count); measures denying the opponent's cheapest next steals, sign positive = denial."""
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    my = (owner == 1).astype(np.float64)
    opp = (owner == -1).astype(np.float64)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    A = adjacency.astype(np.float64)
    deg = np.maximum(A.sum(axis=1), 1.0)

    my_n = A @ my
    opp_n = A @ opp
    # opponent-reachable empties = adjacent to an opponent cell
    oppreach = empty & (opp_n >= 1)

    # gap: how many more opp neighbours than mine (after my claim, mine +1 where candidate adjacent)
    # candidate c supplies +1 to my_n on cells adjacent to c
    cand_adj = A[moves]                      # (k, N)
    my_after = my_n[None, :] + cand_adj      # (k, N)
    gap_before = opp_n[None, :] - my_n[None, :]      # (k,N) same for all rows
    gap_after = opp_n[None, :] - my_after            # (k,N)

    # cells one claim from being stolen: opponent leads by exactly 1 before, and I don't already tie/lead after
    threat = oppreach[None, :] & (gap_before == 1.0) & (gap_after >= 0.0)
    # denial value: candidate only counts if it is adjacent (closes the gap partially)
    closes = (cand_adj > 0) & (gap_after < gap_before)
    w = (pts / 5.0)[None, :] / deg[None, :]
    val = (threat & closes).astype(np.float64) * w
    return np.clip(np.nan_to_num(val.sum(axis=1)), 0.0, 1.0)

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Behind-only flip leverage: when my score is not above the opponent's, for each candidate sum points of opponent non-home cells that would flip (points/5, capped) minus the opponent's frontier dominance on empties it touches, scaled by total points; 0 when ahead."""
    s_me = points[owner == 1].sum()
    s_op = points[owner == -1].sum()
    if s_me > s_op:
        return np.zeros(len(moves))

    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    total = max(pts.sum(), 1.0)
    my = (owner == 1).astype(np.float64)
    opp = (owner == -1).astype(np.float64)
    empty = (owner == 0).astype(np.float64)
    A = adjacency.astype(np.float64)

    my_n = A @ my
    opp_n = A @ opp

    cand_adj = A[moves]                        # (k, N)
    my_after = my_n[None, :] + cand_adj        # (k, N)

    # flip gain: opponent non-home cells where my_after >= opp_n
    is_opp = np.broadcast_to((owner == -1)[None, :], my_after.shape).copy()
    is_opp[:, homes[1]] = False
    flips = is_opp & (my_after >= opp_n[None, :])
    gain = (flips.astype(np.float64) * pts[None, :]).sum(axis=1)

    # in tight/behind spots, deny the opponent's easy value: empties where they dominate
    marg = opp_n[None, :] - my_after            # >0 means opponent dominates that cell
    deny = (np.clip(marg, 0.0, None) * empty[None, :] * pts[None, :]).sum(axis=1)

    vals = (gain - deny) / total
    return np.clip(np.nan_to_num(vals), -1.0, 1.0)

    opp_n = A @ opp

    cand_adj = A[moves]                       # (k, N)
    my_after = my_n[None, :] + cand_adj       # (k, N)

    margin = my_after - opp_n[None, :]        # (k, N)

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """For each candidate: the change it makes to the opponent's future claim options — number of empty cells that only the opponent (not me) can still reach after the claim, weighted by points, minus those only I can reach; scaled by total points, clipped."""

    total = max(pts.sum(), 1.0)
    my = (owner == 1).astype(np.float64)
    opp = (owner == -1).astype(np.float64)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    A = adjacency.astype(np.float64)

    opp_n = A @ opp

    cand_adj = A[moves]                       # (k, N)
    my_after = my_n[None, :] + cand_adj       # (k, N)

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Points x degree-fraction of opponent-reachable empties adjacent to the candidate, plus a quarter-weight on distance-2 ones."""
    pts = points.astype(float)
    my = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    emp0 = (owner == 0)
    A = adjacency.astype(float)
    my_n = A @ my.astype(float)
    opp_n = A @ opp.astype(float)
    deg = A.sum(axis=1)
    N = owner.shape[0]
    A2 = A @ A

    hub = np.clip(deg / 5.0, 0.0, 1.0)
    oppreach = (opp_n >= 1) & emp0
    w = (pts / 5.0) * hub * oppreach.astype(float)
    near = (A[moves] * emp0[None, :]) @ w
    w2 = (pts / 5.0) * oppreach.astype(float)
    far = (A2[moves].astype(float) * emp0[None, :]) @ w2
    return np.clip(near + 0.25 * far, 0.0, 1.0)

import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Net tempo with flip-fold: for each candidate, points^2-weighted empty cells I would strictly dominate after my claim, minus those the opponent still dominates/tie, MINUS a half-weight on opponent non-home cells that would actually flip to me (points^2 weighted) — rewards claims whose flips change the tempo balance, scaled by total squared points."""
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    w = pts * pts
    total = max(w.sum(), 1.0)
    my = (owner == 1).astype(np.float64)
    opp = (owner == -1).astype(np.float64)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    adj = adjacency.astype(np.float64)

    my_n = adj @ my
    opp_n = adj @ opp

    cand_adj = adj[moves]                       # (k, N)
    my_after = my_n[None, :] + cand_adj         # (k, N)

    win = (my_after > opp_n[None, :]) & empty[None, :]
    lose = (my_after < opp_n[None, :]) & empty[None, :]
    tempo = ((win.astype(np.float64) - lose.astype(np.float64)) * w[None, :]).sum(axis=1)

    # flip term: opponent non-home cells that would flip given the claim
    opp_home = homes[1]
    is_opp_nbr = cand_adj.astype(bool) & (opp[None, :] > 0)
    is_opp_nbr[:, opp_home] = False
    flips = (my_n + 1.0) >= opp_n                # (N,) cells that flip
    flip_w = (is_opp_nbr & flips[None, :]).astype(np.float64) * w[None, :]
    flip_term = flip_w.sum(axis=1)

    vals = (tempo - 0.5 * flip_term) / total
    return np.clip(np.nan_to_num(vals), -1.0, 1.0)

    opp = (owner == -1)
    A = adjacency.astype(np.int32)
    own_nbr = A @ own.astype(np.int32)   # (N,)
    opp_nbr = A @ opp.astype(np.int32)   # (N,)

    is_opp_nbr[:, opp_home] = False
    flips = (own_nbr + 1) >= opp_nbr                # (N,)
    gain = (is_opp_nbr & flips[None, :]).astype(np.float64) * pts[None, :]

    flips = (my_n + 1.0) >= opp_n             # (N,)
    flip_val = (is_opp_nbr & flips[None, :]).astype(np.float64) @ (pts / 5.0)

    # risk: opponent-dominated neighbours of the candidate (opp_nbr > my_nbr on that cell)
    danger_cell = np.clip(opp_n - my_n, 0.0, None)  # (N,)
    risk = cand_adj.astype(np.float64) @ danger_cell

    vals = (flip_val - risk) / 3.0
    return np.clip(np.nan_to_num(vals), -1.0, 1.0)

feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """For each candidate: points/5 of empty cells reachable by the opponent within 2 hops whose opponent-neighbour count exceeds mine by exactly 1 (one claim from falling), weighted by 1/deg of the empty cell and by how much the candidate reduces that gap (each candidate-adjacency supplying +1 to the count); measures denying the opponent's cheapest next steals, sign positive = denial."""
    pts = points.astype(np.float64)
    my = (owner == 1).astype(np.float64)
    opp = (owner == -1).astype(np.float64)
    empty = (owner == 0)
    A = adjacency.astype(np.float64)
    deg = np.maximum(A.sum(axis=1), 1.0)

    my_n = A @ my
    opp_n = A @ opp
    # opponent-reachable empties = adjacent to an opponent cell
    oppreach = empty & (opp_n >= 1)

    # gap: how many more opp neighbours than mine (after my claim, mine +1 where candidate adjacent)
    # candidate c supplies +1 to my_n on cells adjacent to c
    cand_adj = A[moves]                      # (k, N)
    my_after = my_n[None, :] + cand_adj      # (k, N)
    gap_before = opp_n[None, :] - my_n[None, :]      # (k,N) same for all rows
    gap_after = opp_n[None, :] - my_after            # (k,N)

    # cells one claim from being stolen: opponent leads by exactly 1 before, and I don't already tie/lead after
    threat = oppreach[None, :] & (gap_before == 1.0) & (gap_after >= 0.0)
    # denial value: candidate only counts if it is adjacent (closes the gap partially)
    closes = (cand_adj > 0) & (gap_after < gap_before)
    w = (pts / 5.0)[None, :] / deg[None, :]
    val = (threat & closes).astype(np.float64) * w
    return np.clip(np.nan_to_num(val.sum(axis=1)), 0.0, 1.0)

feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, points, adjacency, homes, turn):
    """Sum over empty cells adjacent to candidate (and at 2 hops, half weight) of p[e]/deg[e] gated by d_me<=d_opp<4, scaled by 1/3, clipped to [0,1]."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    p = points.astype(float) / 5.0
    deg = adjacency.sum(1).astype(float)
    inv_deg = 1.0 / np.maximum(deg, 1.0)
    my = (owner == 1)
    opp = (owner == -1)
    empty = (owner == 0)

    A = adjacency.astype(float)

    def bfs(seeds):
        # vectorised BFS up to depth 4 over empty cells
        d = np.full(N, 4, dtype=int)
        frontier = seeds & empty
        d[frontier] = 0
        for step in range(1, 4):
            # neighbours of current frontier
            reach = (A @ frontier.astype(float)) > 0
            new = reach & empty & (d > step)
            if not new.any():
                break
            d[new] = step
            frontier = new
        return d

    d_me = bfs(my)
    d_opp = bfs(opp)

    gate = (d_me <= d_opp) & (d_opp < 4) & empty
    w = p * inv_deg * gate.astype(float)  # per empty cell weight

    A2 = A @ A
    two_hop = (A2 > 0) & (~adjacency)

    moves = np.asarray(moves)
    # s1: adjacent empties
    s1 = (adjacency[moves].astype(float) @ w)
    # s2: exactly two hops (not adjacent)
    s2 = 0.5 * (two_hop[moves].astype(float) @ w)

    val = (s1 + s2) / 3.0
    val = np.clip(val, 0.0, 1.0)
    return val

idea.hypothesis: On web (degree 3) the policy's hub features fail because they count every opponent-reachable empty, most of which I cannot win anyway. Filtering those empties by a degree-2 reach gate (I arrive no later than the opponent, d_me <= d_opp, capped at 4) and weighting them by points/deg should isolate the genuine cut cells; if f088 was flat because it lacked exactly this gate, this probe will move web cost.

Compute d_me: BFS from my-owned cells (distance 0), expanding only into empty cells, capped at 4 (unreached = 4); d_opp likewise from opponent-owned cells. For each candidate v: s1 = sum over empty e with adjacency[v,e] of p[e] * (1/max(deg[e],1)) * (d_me[e] <= d_opp[e]) * (d_opp[e] < 4); s2 = 0.5 * the same sum over empty e that are at exactly two hops from v (i.e. (A@A)[v,e] > 0 and adjacency[v,e] == False). value = (s1 + s2)/3, clipped to [0,1]. One column.

feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Sum over opponent non-home cells u adjacent to candidate v that would flip (margin>=0) of the points/5 of empty cells e adjacent to u with opp_nbr[e]==1, divided by 2, clipped to [0,1]."""
    p = points.astype(float) / 5.0
    mine = (owner == 1).astype(float)
    opp = (owner == -1).astype(float)
    my_nbr = adjacency @ mine
    opp_nbr = adjacency @ opp
    margin = my_nbr + 1.0 - opp_nbr

    empty = (owner == 0)
    # w[u] = sum over empty e adjacent to u with opp_nbr[e]==1 of p[e]
    sole_access = empty & (opp_nbr == 1)
    w = adjacency @ (p * sole_access.astype(float))

    # flip mask per cell u (independent of candidate except adjacency)
    flippable = (owner == -1) & (margin >= 0)
    flippable[homes[1]] = False

    # value(v) = sum_u adjacency[v,u] * flippable[u] * w[u]
    contrib = flippable.astype(float) * w
    vals = adjacency[np.asarray(moves)] @ contrib
    vals = vals / 2.0
    return np.clip(vals, 0.0, 1.0)

feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """phase*(exposure tempo) + (1-phase)*(flip tempo), phase = remaining-empties fraction."""
    N = owner.shape[0]
    p = points.astype(float) / 5.0
    mine = (owner == 1).astype(float)
    opp = (owner == -1).astype(float)
    my_nbr = adjacency @ mine
    opp_nbr = adjacency @ opp
    margin = my_nbr + 1.0 - opp_nbr

    empty = (owner == 0)
    opp_nonhome = (owner == -1)
    opp_nonhome[homes[1]] = False

    # exposure: empty neighbours e that I would strictly dominate after my claim
    expo_mask = empty[None, :] & adjacency[moves] & ((my_nbr[None, :] + 1.0) > opp_nbr[None, :])
    expo = (expo_mask * p[None, :]).sum(axis=1) / 3.0
    expo = np.clip(expo, 0.0, 1.0)

    # flip: opponent non-home neighbours u with margin >= 0
    flip_mask = opp_nonhome[None, :] & adjacency[moves] & (margin[None, :] >= 0.0)
    flip = (flip_mask * p[None, :]).sum(axis=1) / 3.0
    flip = np.clip(flip, 0.0, 1.0)

    phase = (N - 2 - turn) / max(N - 2, 1)
    return phase * expo + (1.0 - phase) * flip

idea.hypothesis: f022 (exposure tempo) is the largest single lever (x0: -10.8) but its weight is constant over the game, and the phase-constant weight is exactly what a linear sum cannot vary. Blending exposure tempo in the opening into flip tempo as empties run out lets one column bias the trade-off of early growth against late denial; if the wrong half is currently over-weighted late, this should show up as cost on the flip-heavy hex family.

feature.code:
import numpy as np

def feature(moves, owner, homes, points, adjacency, turn):
    """Sum of points/5 of empty neighbours of each candidate that currently have zero owned neighbours, divided by 3, clipped to [0,1]."""
    mine = (owner == 1).astype(np.float64)
    my_nbr = adjacency @ mine  # owned-neighbour count per cell
    p = points.astype(np.float64) / 5.0
    empty = (owner == 0)
    fresh = empty & (my_nbr == 0)
    fresh_p = np.where(fresh, p, 0.0)
    vals = adjacency[moves] @ fresh_p  # sum of p[e] over fresh empty neighbours
    vals = vals / 3.0
    return np.clip(vals, 0.0, 1.0)
